title.en: Let an event timeline own operational state

summary: Model operations as timestamped events and derive every frame from the timeline, so playback can be scrubbed and questioned.
objective: Choose a state model for operational scenes that supports seeking, pausing and auditing rather than only forward motion.
applies_when: Items move through a sorter, line, dock or queue over time.
The user can pause, scrub, speed up or step through a process.
Counts, utilisation or waiting times are displayed alongside the animation.
example_prompts: Play back the sorting run and let me jump to any minute.
Show the dock schedule as it actually happened, with pause and step.
negative_signals: Ambient background motion that represents no process.
Continuous physical simulation, where the state is a field rather than a list of events.
not_for: Ambient background motion that represents no process.
Continuous physical simulation, where the state is a field rather than a list of events.

principles: An operational scene answers questions about time. If state exists only as the current position of moving meshes, the scene cannot answer where was this item at minute seven.

Events are the facts; animation interpolates between them. A timestamp alone is not a complete cursor, because several events can share one time and the states between them differ, so the cursor is a timestamp plus a position in a stable event order. Deriving the picture from that cursor makes scrubbing, replay and speed changes exact rather than approximate.
Derived statistics must come from the same event stream as the visuals, otherwise the counter and the picture can disagree without anyone noticing.
Event data may be recorded, generated by a scheduler or invented for illustration, and the scene should say which, because those carry different authority.
implementation: Define the event vocabulary first: arrival, start of service, completion, departure, failure, each with entity identity and timestamp.

Render frame state as a pure function of the cursor: a timestamp plus a tie-break index into a stable event order. Say whether a bare time query means the state before the first event at that time, after all of them, or at a selected event, and keep that convention fixed. Reconstructing from a snapshot plus ordered replay is an equally valid implementation of the same function.
Keep the interpolation honest: a straight glide between two events is a display choice, and any curved path or acceleration should be labelled as presentation.

Compute queue lengths, utilisation and waiting times from the event list at the same complete cursor used by the scene, rather than incrementing counters during playback or collapsing tied events to a bare timestamp.
Record where the events came from with the artifact: measured log, generated schedule or authored illustration.
observable_checks: Scrub backwards and forwards to the same complete cursor from different directions and confirm the scene is identical both times; where several events share a timestamp, confirm stepping visits them in the declared order rather than collapsing them.
Pause and compare the visible items against the computed queue lengths and counters.
Change playback speed and confirm reported times and rates stay in model units rather than following the display rate.

Seek past a long idle period and confirm the state matches the requested complete cursor. Direct evaluation, replay from the initial state, and snapshot plus ordered replay are valid reconstruction strategies.

creative_affordances: Presentation is open: conveyor metaphors, abstract lanes or a spatial Gantt view all work over the same event model.
Illustrative event data is legitimate for a demonstration when it is labelled as such.
known_limits: Authored state-model guidance; no runtime playback has been exercised for this record.
It does not provide a simulation engine, a scheduling algorithm or any performance claim about a real facility.
